demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Delays' suggests a broad expectancy of external danger from uncertainty/delays, which fits poorly with the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; the rest of the profile centers on guilt, recall-based distress, and hypervigilance rather than delay-specific threat meanings.

issues.item: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For a patient whose trauma was accidentally injuring another, the appraisals presented otherwise focus on guilt, inadequacy, and permanent moral/personal change. A loss of trust in one's body usually implies prominent bodily injury, dissociation, panic-like symptoms, or functional impairment, none of which are represented elsewhere in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies.

vignette:
Gerald is a 62-year-old married man of European descent who has worked as a bank teller for nearly two decades. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 58, seeking help approximately fourteen months after the incident that, in his own words, "broke something in me that hasn't healed."

The event occurred on a busy Friday afternoon at the bank. A long-standing customer - a man Gerald had greeted by name for years, whose children's savings accounts Gerald had helped open - became agitated during a transaction dispute. As Gerald leaned across the counter to pass documents, the man stumbled backward, lost his footing on a recently mopped floor, and struck his head against a marble pillar. The sound was immediate and terrible. Gerald had reached out instinctively, his hand grazing the man's shoulder a fraction of a second too late. The customer sustained a serious traumatic brain injury and spent weeks in intensive care. He survived, but Gerald was told he would never fully recover. Gerald has replayed that moment of contact - his fingers brushing fabric, the inadequate reach - thousands of times since.

In the weeks that followed, fragments of the memory began surfacing without warning: the wet sound of impact, the particular stillness of the man's body on the marble floor, the faces of other customers frozen in shock. These intrusive pieces arrived suddenly and then vanished, leaving Gerald shaking at his teller window or gripping the edge of the bathroom sink at home. Each time the memory returned, the terror he had felt in that moment returned with it - not as recollection but as re-experience - and alongside the terror came a wave of guilt so acute it felt physical. This combination of terror and guilt kept Gerald's nervous system in a state of chronic arousal. He found himself unable to fall asleep without scanning the house, unable to sit quietly in the evenings, hypervigilant to sounds and movement in a way that exhausted his wife and bewildered him. The sustained threat state, in turn, seemed to lower the threshold for intrusion: the more alert he remained, the more readily the memory broke through, and the more it broke through, the more alert he became.

Gerald returned to work after three weeks, which he now recognises was too soon. The bank environment - where he stands behind the same counter, handles the same transactions, and sees many of the same familiar faces - became saturated with cues. Customers he recognised, people connected even loosely to the man who was injured, triggered a cascade of self-accusation. He had come to believe, with quiet certainty, that he was inadequate - that a competent person, a person of sound reflexes and good judgment, would have caught the man in time. When he saw related customers at his window, this belief crystallised instantly: he was the teller who had failed, and everyone in the bank knew it. These encounters with known people fed directly into his appraisals of permanent damage, and those appraisals in turn made him more sensitised to the triggers themselves - he began scanning the lobby for familiar faces before his shift, dreading the moment of recognition. Even stress at the counter, the ordinary pressure of a queue or a disputed balance, now carried the weight of that afternoon, pulling him back toward the memory and the guilt embedded in it.

An unexpected touch became its own particular ordeal. When a colleague placed a hand on his arm to get his attention one morning, Gerald flinched so violently that the woman stepped back in alarm. He was unable to explain it to her. He had come to see his reactions - the flinching, the sleeplessness, the inability to relax even at home on a Sunday - as further evidence of how thoroughly he had been damaged. He was, he believed, a lousy coper, and this belief had begun to isolate him from his wife, who could not reach him in the evenings, and from colleagues who had quietly stopped confiding in him.

What finally brought Gerald to seek help was his wife's tearful observation that she felt she had lost him. He arrived at the intake appointment hoping, more than anything, to stop feeling like a man who had irreparably broken both another person and himself.
